title: The Hole
intro: The world is on fire and your retirement is a lie. Welcome back to The Daily Dagoth. I'm Dagoth Ur. With me: Rosa. And Jessica, who I can already see vibrating at a frequency that suggests she has found something she was not supposed to find.
outro: That's the episode. Jessica, I need to go sit in a dark room now. Rosa, thank you for keeping a single shred of optimism alive for twenty-six minutes. Dagoth Ur, signing off. Share this one. Especially to anyone who believes their insurance policy is an asset class.

segments.topic: Opening — The Thing Nobody Is Looking At

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Jessica. What did you find.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Okay so — Nick Nemeth. Mispriced Assets Substack. He dropped part two of 'No More Boomer Communism' and I have been sitting with this for four days and I need everyone to know: it is worse than part one.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Everything is worse than everything now. That's just the news cycle.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Rosa, I know. But this is structurally worse. Part one was about private credit. The thing everyone's watching. Part two — Nick is saying private credit is not the main event. It's the match. The actual bomb is insurance.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Nick called it the trigger versus the hole. Everyone is watching the fuse. The building is somewhere else.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Hold on. The boring insurance companies? The ones with the print brochures and the waiting rooms and the guy at the counter who asks about your beneficiaries? Those are the systemic risk?

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: The life and annuity industry specifically. Ten trillion dollars in assets. Ten trillion. Larger than the entire US banking system before 2008. And the cushion keeping the lights on — the actual surplus — is six hundred and fifty-eight billion dollars. Six point five percent margin.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Ten trillion in assets. Less than seven hundred billion in actual money behind it. That is not a financial institution. That is a confidence trick with better typography.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Six point five percent.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: And that is before you account for affiliated reinsurance. Which — okay, I need to explain this part because it's where it gets — it's good. It's an elegant hack.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Jessica. You said 'good' and 'elegant hack' in the same sentence about a fraud mechanism.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: I said it was elegant. It is elegant. From a certain angle. Here's how it works: an insurance company wants its balance sheet to look healthier than it is. So it creates — pays a small premium to — a reinsurance company it owns entirely. A captive. That captive issues an XOL contract. Excess of loss. The contract says: if our assets drop below a certain level, the captive covers the loss.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: So they're insuring themselves against their own failure.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: They are insuring themselves against their own failure and then showing the policy as an asset on the balance sheet.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: The liability disappears. Replaced by a document that says the problem has been solved. The problem has not been solved. The money does not exist. The regulator looks at the document and says looks fine to me.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Is there a strike price? Like, at what point does this actually pay out?

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Rosa. You're going to hate this.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Tell me anyway.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Most of these XOL contracts have a negative strike. Meaning the assets would have to go negative before the coverage activates. Negative five dollars.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: That is not insurance. That is a participation trophy.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: And this is not one bad actor.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Athene. Equitable. Lincoln National. MetLife. Prudential. Brookfield. All doing it. The entire industry is running on reinsurance that is, in the charitable interpretation, inadequate. In the accurate interpretation —

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Fraudulent.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: I was going to say creative accounting but yes. That.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Okay. How big is the hole? Just give me the number.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: One point five trillion dollars in affiliated reinsurance across the US life and annuity industry. Nick's researcher — Tom Gober, forensic accountant, forty-two years, time undercover with the FBI — he used NAIC statutory data compiled by SNL Financial. One point five trillion.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Against a total capital surplus of six hundred and fifty-eight billion.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Which means affiliated reinsurance is two hundred and thirty-five percent of the actual surplus.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: I'm sorry. Two hundred and thirty-five percent of the actual — how is that even possible on paper?

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: It's possible because no one is auditing it. If you stripped the affiliated reinsurance off every balance sheet simultaneously — not a crisis, just a correction — twenty-nine of the top thirty US life and annuity insurers would be insolvent.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: The thirtieth is probably New York Life. They're actually mutual. They're just old and scared of everything.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Twenty-nine of thirty. And I own some of these companies. In my retirement account. I just realized I own some of these companies.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Rosa, everyone owns these companies. They're investment grade. They pay dividends. Your target-date fund owns them.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: I hate that you're right.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: The NAIC has rules. Fifty percent of surplus, or ten percent of assets. Whichever is lower. That's the legal cap on affiliated reinsurance.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Athene is running at twenty-six times the legal maximum.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Twenty-six times —

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: They got Iowa and Arizona to sign waivers. Two state commissioners. That is the regulatory response to discovering the largest accounting fraud in US history. They found two friendly people and got permission.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Please sir may we have permission.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: That is literally the quote from the video. Nick used those words. Please sir may we have permission.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: And the ratings agencies?

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Athene has a double-A rating. MetLife has a double-A rating. Investment grade. On companies that, under honest accounting, would be in receivership.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: And the ratings agencies are paid by the companies they're rating.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Which does not appear in their marketing materials.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: So we have fraudulent accounting, captured regulators, compromised ratings agencies. What's the actual mechanism that breaks this? Because if it's this bad and still standing, something is holding it up.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Steve Eisman. Yes, that Steve Eisman. He went on CNBC two weeks ago and called this the biggest short of his career.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: The stock went up after he said it.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: The stock went up.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: The man who called Enron before anyone said fraud — his career-defining short — and the stock goes up.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: That tells you the CDS market does not exist.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Credit default swaps on insurance companies. There's no liquid underlying. No clear reference instrument. Eisman is trying to build a book — MetLife at ninety-three bid on the five-year, Lincoln National at one-fifty-five. He's trying to create a vehicle to bet against this. And the prime brokers won't build it.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Because if the vehicle exists, someone has to explain why the double-A rated companies underneath it are worth less than par.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: So the problem isn't that the truth is hidden. The problem is everyone who could act on it is also holding the thing that blows up if they do.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Rosa.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: What.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: That was really good.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: She stole your bit.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: I know. I'm not happy about it.

segments.topic: The Brookfield Example — A Real Case Study

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Is there a concrete example? Something with actual numbers.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Oh, I have something with actual numbers. Brookfield. They acquired American Equity Investment Life — life insurance company, roughly eight billion in assets. Created three captive reinsurance subsidiaries. Very standard. Very normal.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Very normal so far.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: One of them — AEL Re Vermont — shows an XOL asset of one point four eight billion dollars on Brookfield's balance sheet.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: The premium they paid to create it was eleven point six million dollars.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Eleven million dollars.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Sixty basis points. Creates the appearance of one point four eight billion in coverage. Now, the XOL contract — the way these work — it covers losses below a certain threshold, but most of them have a negative strike, meaning the assets would have to go negative before the coverage actually — I'm losing people already, aren't I.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: You lost me at eleven million dollars creating the appearance of one point four eight billion. I'm still there.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Let me take that one. The strike price was negative five dollars. Meaning this coverage only activates if American Equity goes to zero. At which point the counterparty is also bankrupt. This is not insurance. That is a participation trophy.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Brookfield did not invent this. Nick specifically says in the video: they're not that guy. They didn't originate this scheme. They just participated in it with great enthusiasm.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Which is the most honest thing anyone has said in this episode.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Where's the money actually sitting? If it's not on the balance sheet, where is it?

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Bermuda. Cayman Islands. Barbados. Ireland.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Places with no US regulatory jurisdiction.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Correct. No US court can subpoena it. They can write whatever they want on the balance sheet and no one forces the question.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: And US courts can't reach it.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Cannot reach it.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Nick's phrase — I love this phrase — he says the money does not have to exist. As long as nobody forces the question, it doesn't.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: The offshore structure is not a tax optimization. It is a visibility optimization. For fraud.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: For fraud.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: For fraud.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Now here's the part I find really funny. The growth of affiliated reinsurance is being driven by the weakest balance sheets. Because only the companies that are in trouble need to move liabilities offshore. The healthy ones don't need to.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: The growth in affiliated reinsurance is a canary in the coal mine.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: The sicker the company, the more creative the accounting.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: And nobody is connecting those two facts.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Nobody is connecting those two facts because everyone connecting them would have to explain why they're not doing anything about it.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Including the ratings agencies.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Including the ratings agencies.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Including the ratings agencies.

segments.topic: The Trigger — How It Actually Unwinds

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: So how does it break? Walk me through the actual mechanism.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: It starts with what everyone's already watching — private credit defaults accelerating. That's the trigger. Defaults go up, mark-to-market losses hit the balance sheets. Companies that were barely holding on start showing cracks.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Then the ratings agencies, who should have downgraded these companies years ago, finally act. A downgrade to triple-B minus sounds abstract. What it actually means is capital calls from the PE funds. Because the PE funds have contractual provisions that require the insurance company to maintain certain capital ratios. Downgrade hits, capital call goes out, they have to raise money immediately.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: To raise money they sell assets.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: In an illiquid market, selling assets fast means fire-sale prices.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Fire-sale prices trigger more downgrades. More downgrades trigger more capital calls. And then —

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: And then you hit the XOL assets. The ones that were supposed to cover the losses. The ones with the negative five dollar strike prices. They don't cover anything. The capital reserves were phantom.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: And now you have a ten trillion dollar industry with no cushion, and the losses flow straight to the state guarantee funds.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: State guarantee funds. Those are the things that backstop insurance policies if a company fails. They're funded by — ?

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Nothing. Pre-funded balance is zero. Unlike FDIC insurance, which has a pre-funded deposit insurance fund, state life insurance guarantee funds have no money set aside. When the claims come in, the state pays out of general revenue.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Which is another way of saying —

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Your taxes. Or the Fed creates the money. Same destination, different printing press.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Jerome Powell, to his partial credit, admitted in the two thousand twenty-four Financial Stability Report that the growth of private credit poses risks to financial stability. He said yes. He just declined to specify the size of the hole. Which is a bit like pointing at your house from across the street and saying yes there is a fire, we are not going to say which room.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: I think about that quote a lot.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Of course you do.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: He knows. He knows the size of the hole. He just can't say it without causing the thing he's describing.

segments.topic: Burry, Chanos, Eisman — The Smart Money Speaks

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Okay but. Burry posted. Michael Burry. The Big Short guy. He posted about insurance. Nick quotes the tweet directly: every time anyone looked, Scottish Re, AIG, it's all the same. There is nothing there.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Burry doesn't tweet before he does the work. If he's posting, he's already positioned.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Which means the short is already on. He's not announcing a trade. He's leaving a record. The way someone leaves a record when they've already pulled the fire alarm and want to make sure people know they didn't start the fire.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: He's covered.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: He's covered and he's telling you where to look. That's the Burry move. He always gives you just enough to find it yourself.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Jim Chanos — who called Enron before anyone was willing to say the word fraud — called this the golden age of fraud.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: And he's not wrong. The private credit boom gave everyone cover. PE firms collecting fees, insurance companies collecting premium, ratings agencies collecting rating fees, regulators collecting salaries. Nobody had an incentive to look.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: The fraud was hiding in the Bermudas and Caymans where no US court could reach it.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Where the accounting standards don't require the same disclosures as domestic filings.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: And where everyone involved had a financial reason to leave it alone.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: So the choice is between fraud and regulatory failure.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Those are the two options on the menu.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: The version where this unravels on purpose with federal oversight, and the version where it unravels on its own and we discover the hole is three times deeper than anyone admitted.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Wonderful. Both options are great.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Let's talk about the title. 'No More Boomer Communism.' What does that actually mean beyond the obvious media appeal.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Nick defines it precisely. Boomer communism is a system where private parties collect the gains and the public absorbs the losses. That was defined benefit pensions — raided, underfunded, backstopped by the government. That was savings and loan associations in the 1980s. That was the mortgage crisis in 2008. That was Social Security, perpetually one congressional fix away from collapse.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Every generation has had at least one encounter with this arrangement.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: The baby boomers designed the entire system.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: And insurance is the last unaudited defined-benefit machine still running.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: The last one where the public pays for private losses and nobody's had the political will to look.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Banks were broken and reformed — imperfectly, but visibly. Hedge funds got Archegosed in 2021. Private equity has been getting scrutiny for years. Insurance has been invisible. And what Tom Gober found is that the accounting is worse than anything we found in banking. Not because insurance people are more dishonest than bankers.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Because they had more time to build the architecture.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Exactly.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: The policyholders bear the actuarial risk. The PE firms collect the management fees. The state backstops the losses. The Fed prints the money. And every link in that chain says the next link has the money.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Until you pull the thread and discover the whole thing is held together with XOL contracts that have negative five dollar strike prices and eleven million dollar premiums.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Nick says the only way this ends well is if someone in power decides to look.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: A single federal investigation. One congressional hearing with subpoena power. Crack open the captives, force mark-to-market valuation on the affiliated reinsurance.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: The NAIC already has the data. SNL Financial already compiles it. Gober already used it. The information is not hidden. It is simply not being acted on.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: And right now there's no evidence anyone in power wants to look.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Correct. Because looking would require admitting the problem is large enough to matter. And that would require doing something about it. And doing something about it means telling a generation of retirees that the system they were promised was a rough approximation of the truth.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Nobody in Washington wants to have that conversation until they absolutely have to have it.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Which means they're hoping it solves itself.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: Which means they're hoping it solves itself. Which it won't.

segments.topic: The Closing Question — Is There a Trade?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: So what's the play here? For anyone listening who's not Steve Eisman. What's the actual action item.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: For most people: know what you actually own. If you have a variable annuity, an indexed annuity, any product where the insurance company is taking your money and putting it in private credit or CLOs — you are not holding a bond. You are holding a promise from a company that may be insolvent in any meaningful sense of the word.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: If you work at a state insurance guarantee fund, or you interact with state pension systems, this is your problem more directly than most. The state backstop is not a blank check. It is a line item in a budget that does not have the money.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: When the calls come in, the options are: raise taxes, cut services, or ask the federal government.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: None of which are fast or popular.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: None of which work quickly or equitably in a crisis, historically speaking.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: And for the trading desk crowd — the CDS market doesn't exist yet in any usable form. Eisman is trying to build it. If he succeeds, you can buy protection on MetLife or Lincoln National the same way you bought protection on mortgage-backed securities in 2007.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: If he doesn't succeed?

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: If he doesn't succeed, the unraveling will be visible in other ways first. Watch for downgrade cascades in the PE-backed insurers. Watch for the ratings agencies being forced to explain their double-A marks on companies that can't produce honest balance sheets.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: The canary won't sing quietly.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: So the answer for regular people is: you can't trade this, you can't short this, you probably can't see the full scope of it.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: You can just know that it's there.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: You can know that it's there. You can not be surprised when the story breaks. And you can ask the question that Nick is asking, that Eisman is asking, that Burry is apparently positioning around: what happens when the money is supposed to be real, and nobody can find it?

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: Because that question has an answer. The answer is not good. And the answer is not quiet.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Nick's last line in the video — he says: I may be vigorous but I'm not that smart. And then he says: Michael, you can figure this out. Take your sweet time.

lines.speaker: Dagoth Ur
lines.text: He's talking to Burry.

lines.speaker: Jessica
lines.text: He's talking to Burry. He's saying: I found it. I showed you where to look. Now it's your move.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: And Burry's move is apparently already made.
